title: Australian government paper proposes opt-out for AI training
content:
AI companies could use creators' work without paying them under leaked government copyright proposal
AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic would be allowed to train their models on online content without paying its creators as long as they struck deals with enough rights holders, under one copyright reform plan put forward in government documents seen by the ABC.
The attorney-general's department made the proposal as part of consultations with rights-holders' groups earlier this month, which would make inclusion in AI training opt-out by default.
The revelation comes as the Albanese government tries to break a months-long gridlock over reforms to copyright law.
AI models are typically trained on enormous amounts of data scraped from the internet, including copyrighted materials taken without their owners' permissions, to the chagrin of creative groups.
Uncertainty about the legality of training models this way has been a sticking point for the government's efforts to attract AI companies to make the major investments in Australia that would come with AI training efforts.
ACT independent senator David Pocock pressed the government about its previously unrevealed plans in the Senate today.
"This would be huge and mean that our legal system would protect AI companies first and Australians second. The burden should not fall on Australians to defend the rights over content they hold, create and invest in," he said.
Senator Don Farrell said that he would need to consult with Attorney-General Michelle Rowland on the topic, but reiterated the government's stance against watering down copyright.
"The government has taken a deep interest in artificial intelligence with a view to maximising the benefits that come from this new technology, but on the other hand making sure […] we get the best possible results for the Australian community," he said.
A spokesperson for Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said the government was continuing to consult with creators, media organisations and AI companies on a range of options to ensure any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation.
OpenAI confirmed that it had been part of consultations about proposals.
"We are committed to engaging constructively throughout this process with the government, creators and industry on an approach that is practical, sustainable and right for Australia," a spokesperson said.
Two proposals to pave way for AI training in Australia
Slides of the confidential consultation, titled "AI on Australian Terms", seen by the ABC, revealed two options presented to rights-holder groups earlier this month.
Both options would give copyright owners an opt-out if they wanted to keep their online material out of AI training without a licence.
The first proposal sets out two possible ways to pay copyright owners, in addition to voluntary deals with AI companies.
One would give AI companies legal permission to use "unprotected" — meaning content whose owners had not opted-out — online material for training as long as they had made payments to a central body and met other conditions. This body would distribute the money to registered copyright owners.
This first proposal would give the option for AI companies to get a license for training by directly doing deals with Australian collecting groups that represent copyright owners.
This would clear the way for companies to train on content from industries such as music or writing, including content that belongs to people who are not members of the groups who received payments.
The alternative proposal put forward by the Attorney-General's Department would instead require AI companies to strike deals with a minimum number of companies for a minimum period before receiving legal permission to train on unprotected material online.
These deals would be negotiated between the AI companies and the rights-holder companies, the slides say: "No additional $ would be payable to creators or rights holders beyond deals negotiated to achieve quota."
The slides also say the proposals include other protections, including penalties for ignoring opt-outs, "protections for Indigenous Cultural and intellectual Property", as well as transparency and audit requirements.
It would also require AI companies to make "best efforts" to ensure they were not training on pirated material.
Material without those protections could be used even if it was covered by copyright.
The slides say the options would address AI companies' concerns about the "long tail": openly available online material for which striking voluntary deals is unrealistic or impossible.
These options would "improve legal certainty for AI companies and bring advantage of AI training home for Australians" while also "upholding Prime Minister's commitment to a strong and vibrant Australian creative and media sector", the slides say.
Major AI companies say copyright is a hurdle to Australian investment
OpenAI's vice president of global policy Ann O'Leary told The Australian that copyright settings were preventing the company from building an AI training centre in Australia.
"We will not be able to build a … training centre here if the copyright law is as it exists," she said while on a trip to Australia.
An OpenAI spokesperson told the ABC it had been taking part in consultation on the copyright reforms.
"Australia has enormous potential to benefit from AI, and we want to work for and with Australia to help realise Australia's AI ambitions. This is truly a once-in-a-generation opportunity for Australia's economy and it's crucial the country gets this right," they said.
Anthropic had made similar advances to the federal government as early as April, according to a Treasury Freedom of Information (FOI) showing that it was preparing for discussion with the AI company that would say their investment was "contingent" on "clarity" on copyright law.
That briefing said Anthropic could negotiate with larger copyright owners, but argued the "long tail" of smaller owners made identifying and buying licences difficult.
Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles hosed down claims that OpenAI had delivered an ultimatum about copyright.
"It's a historic opportunity for our nation, but we need to be doing it in a way which protects rights holders," Mr Marles told News24 earlier today.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

report.summary: Leaked Australian government proposals would let AI firms train on creators’ online work by default, with copyright owners required to opt out.
report.background: AI models are trained on massive web-scraped datasets, often including copyrighted books, music, articles and images without permission. This legal uncertainty has stalled Australia’s copyright reform debate and complicated efforts to attract major AI investment. OpenAI and Anthropic have linked Australian data-centre or training investment to clearer copyright rules, while creative and media groups warn that defaulting to free training would weaken their rights. The Attorney-General’s Department presented rights-holder groups with confidential options under the banner “AI on Australian Terms.” Both would make AI training opt-out rather than opt-in, aiming to address the “long tail” of online material that is impractical to license individually while offering some compensation, transparency and audit safeguards.
key_points: Both proposals would make copyrighted online content available for AI training by default unless the owner actively opts out. The documents say this would shift the practical burden onto creators to defend and register their rights, though penalties for ignoring opt-outs and protections for Indigenous cultural IP are also floated.

One option would let AI companies train on unprotected material if they pay a central body, which would distribute money to registered copyright owners, or strike direct deals with Australian collecting societies. This could cover works by creators who are not members of those groups.

The alternative would require AI companies to sign deals with a minimum number of rights-holder companies for a minimum period before training on unprotected content. The slides say no extra money would be payable beyond those quota deals.

The plans aim to give AI companies legal certainty and bring training investment to Australia. OpenAI says current copyright law prevents it building a training centre locally, while Anthropic reportedly made investment contingent on clarity.

Political reaction is divided. Independent senator David Pocock says the plan protects AI companies first, while government ministers insist they will not water down copyright and are consulting on meaningful control and fair compensation.
report.impact: For AI companies, the proposals could lower Australian legal risk and unlock data-centre investment, but they still impose opt-out compliance, auditing, transparency and piracy-avoidance duties. Developers may need to document training data, honour exclusion signals and integrate rights registries or licensed feeds, raising operational costs but reducing lawsuit exposure. For creators and regular users, the default shifts from permission to exclusion: unless they opt out, their work may train commercial models, with compensation routed through collective bodies or quota deals that may be indirect or small. Australia could set a global precedent for opt-out AI copyright regimes, intensifying debates in the EU, US and UK.
report.tools: To follow or act on opt-outs, watch Spawning’s Have I Been Trained?, Cloudflare AI Crawl Control and AI Audit, robots.txt and ai.txt exclusion standards, and C2PA content credentials for provenance. Rights registries and collective licensing bodies will also matter, as will open datasets with clear licences. Developers should monitor Australia’s Copyright Agency, APRA AMCOS and similar collecting societies for upcoming licensing schemes.
